reasoning_traces.think:
The derivation of positive patterning in simultaneous stimulus compounds hinges on the interplay between afferent interaction and differential reinforcement. Initially, stimuli A and B are presented together, generating a combined excitation through physiological summation. This summation is not merely additive but is modulated by the generalization gradient, which dictates how excitation spreads across similar stimulus dimensions. When the compound is reinforced, an excitatory potential (E) is established. However, the introduction of differential reinforcement—where the compound is reinforced but individual components are not—necessitates the generation of experimental extinction (Ik). This inhibition acts as a subtractive operator on the generalized excitation of the isolated components. The mathematical core involves solving for the steady-state response where the summed excitation of the compound minus the inherited inhibition exceeds the reaction threshold. The shrinkage of effective reaction values (e.g., from 40 to 30) illustrates the dampening effect of generalization over distance or time. The failure mode arises when the inhibitory gradient overshadows the excitatory summation, causing the compound response to collapse below the critical threshold, thereby negating the patterning effect. This dynamic mirrors complex systems where local reinforcement must overcome global noise and historical decay.
